requirements.requirement: Define the synthetic-data settings relevant to the analysis and explain why their differences matter.
requirements.description: The response should distinguish synthetic data generated by LLMs or programs, uses in pretraining or fine-tuning, and pure-synthetic versus mixed synthetic–real training when those distinctions affect risks or benefits. It should avoid treating all synthetic data and all training regimes as equivalent.

requirements.requirement: Assess the potential data-quality benefits of synthetic data for LLM training or fine-tuning.
requirements.description: The response should explain when synthetic data can increase scale, coverage, diversity, label availability, or representation of rare and edge-case examples. Cost and scalability benefits may be included when they enable these quality improvements, but should not substitute for evidence of improved data or model quality.

requirements.requirement: Assess the data-quality failure modes that synthetic data can introduce and their effects on downstream models.
requirements.description: The response should address relevant risks such as factual or semantic errors, incorrect labels, repetition, low diversity, artifacts, distribution mismatch, contamination, and degradation from repeated synthetic-data training. It should connect these failures to possible effects on accuracy, generalization, or robustness and identify conditions that make them more or less likely.

requirements.requirement: Assess whether and under what conditions synthetic data can reduce harmful bias.
requirements.description: The response should discuss mechanisms such as targeted coverage, rebalancing, counterfactual or fairness-aware generation, filtering, and weighting. It should distinguish a more balanced synthetic dataset from demonstrated improvements in model behavior, and state what comparisons or evidence are needed to support a bias-reduction claim.

requirements.requirement: Assess how synthetic-data generation and use can preserve, introduce, or amplify demographic and representational bias.
requirements.description: The response should cover generator bias, subgroup or class imbalance, stereotypical associations, spurious correlations, minority underrepresentation, and amplification through iterative or large-scale training where relevant. It should distinguish bias measured in generated data from bias observed in the trained model.

requirements.requirement: Explain how to evaluate whether synthetic data is fit for LLM training or fine-tuning using multiple complementary measures.
requirements.description: The response should address relevant dimensions such as factuality, semantic or label correctness, fidelity to the intended distribution, diversity, coverage, training utility, and generalization to held-out real data. It should explain the limitations of statistical, human, model-based, and perplexity-style metrics and warn against treating synthetic-only or generator-aligned tests as sufficient.

requirements.requirement: Specify how to evaluate the representational and fairness effects of using synthetic data.
requirements.description: The response should recommend comparisons with appropriate real-data-only or no-synthetic baselines and subgroup-sensitive evaluation on held-out, preferably real, data. It should consider changes in subgroup performance, error rates, representation, or disparity, rather than treating dataset balance or prompts alone as evidence of fairness improvement.

requirements.requirement: Reach a conditional, evidence-based conclusion about when synthetic data is beneficial or harmful.
requirements.description: The response should relate outcomes to factors such as generator and target-model capability, task and domain, data quantity and composition, synthetic-to-real ratio, curation and filtering, prompting, training regime, and evaluation protocol. It should acknowledge uncertainty and conflicting findings, avoid a universal verdict, and identify practical safeguards or decision criteria for deployment.
